The Rasterization Pipeline

The Problem: Why Standard Plots Break

  • matplotlib / seaborn render one mark per data point — fine at N = 10K, broken at N = 10M+
  • Memory: a 10M-point scatter plot can consume several GB before a pixel is drawn
  • Overplotting hides structure — dense regions look identical to sparse ones
  • The solution: don’t plot points, plot statistics of pixels

The Rasterization Strategy

Traditional pipeline

data (N rows)
  → geometry (N shapes)
    → render (N draw calls)
      → screen pixels

Bottleneck is proportional to N

Rasterization pipeline

data (N rows)
  → canvas grid (W × H bins)
    → aggregate into bins
      → colormap bins → pixels

Bottleneck is proportional to W × H (fixed)

Key insight: the screen has a fixed resolution. Aggregate to pixels before rendering, not after.

How Datashader Works

Code 
flowchart LR
  A[DataFrame <br> N rows] --> B[Canvas <br> W×H grid]
  B --> C[Aggregate <br> count / mean / sum…]
  C --> D[Transfer <br> function / colormap]
  D --> E[Image <br> W×H pixels]

  1. Canvas — define a pixel grid mapped to data coordinates
  2. Aggregate — reduce all points that fall in each pixel to a scalar (default: count)
  3. Transfer function — map aggregates to colors (linear, log, eq-hist)
  4. Embed — return a PNG/RGBA image for display in Jupyter, Bokeh, or HoloViews

Datashader: Minimal Example

Code 
import datashader as ds, colorcet as cc
import hvsampledata as hvs

df = hvs.nyc_taxi_remote("pandas", engine_kwargs={"columns": ['dropoff_x', 'dropoff_y']})

canvas = ds.Canvas(plot_width=500, plot_height=300)
agg = canvas.points(df, 'dropoff_x', 'dropoff_y')
ds.tf.set_background(ds.tf.shade(agg, cmap=cc.fire), "black")
  • Plotting 11,842,094 dropoff locations in NYC
  • What’s being plotted is the total number of dropoffs at locations within each pixel on this canvas
  • This aggregate is then being mapped to colors on a colorscale
  • It’s using latitude and longitude, but without much context
  • Works with pandas, Dask, cuDF (NVIDIA’s GPU-accelerated DataFrame library), Polars (via Arrow)
  • No data is sent to the browser — only the final W×H image

The NYC Taxi data used here is derivative of the other yellow taxi data we’ve used this semester

Datashader: Contexualizing the visualization

Code 
import holoviews as hv
from holoviews.element.tiles import EsriImagery
from holoviews.operation.datashader import datashade
hv.extension('bokeh')

map_tiles  = EsriImagery().opts(alpha=0.5, width=900, height=480, bgcolor='black')
points     = hv.Points(df, ['dropoff_x', 'dropoff_y'])
taxi_trips = datashade(points, x_sampling=1, y_sampling=1, cmap=cc.fire, width=900, height=480)

map_tiles * taxi_trips
ⓘ

We can put our visualization on top of a map, for example. Maps are often provided as raster graphics.

Aggregation Reductions

Reduction Code Use case
Point count ds.count() density maps
Numeric mean ds.mean("value") spatial averages
Any/first value ds.any(), ds.first("col") categorical presence
Count-distinct ds.count_cat("category") multi-class overlays
Min / Max ds.min(), ds.max() range surfaces

Default is count() — most visualizations start here.

Transfer Functions and Colormapping

  • Linear
  • Log
  • Histogram equalization
Code 
# Linear scale — good for uniform density
ds.tf.shade(agg, cmap=cc.blues)
Code 
# Log scale — compresses wide dynamic range
ds.tf.shade(agg, how="log", cmap=cc.kbc)
Code 
# Histogram equalization — reveals structure at all densities
ds.tf.shade(agg, how="eq_hist", cmap=cc.fire)
  • eq_hist is usually the best default for exploratory work — it adapts to the data’s own distribution
  • tf.spread(img, px=1) dilates sparse pixels so they are visible; tf.dynspread adjusts dilation automatically based on point density

Categorical / Multi-Class Plots

# Color each category separately, then compose
from datashader.colors import Sets1to3

agg = canvas.points(df, "dropoff_x", "dropoff_y", ds.count_cat("payment_type"))
img = tf.shade(agg, color_key=Sets1to3)
ds.tf.spread(img, px=1)   # thicken points for visibility
  • Each category gets its own color channel; overlaps alpha-blend
  • Works well for up to ~8–10 classes before colors merge

Integration with HoloViews

HoloViews is a Python library for interactive visualization built on Bokeh (a browser-based plotting engine).

Code 
import holoviews as hv
from holoviews.operation.datashader import datashade, rasterize

hv.extension("bokeh")   # use the Bokeh (interactive) backend

points = hv.Points(df, kdims=["dropoff_x", "dropoff_y"])
datashade(points).opts(width=800, height=600)
ⓘ
  • datashade re-renders on every zoom / pan — aggregation reruns at the new viewport
  • rasterize preserves the aggregate array for further HoloViews operations
  • Result is an interactive plot in Jupyter — no data sent to the browser

Deploying with Panel

Panel is a Python dashboarding library that wraps HoloViews plots into shareable web apps.

import panel as pn

pn.extension()

plot = datashade(hv.Points(df, kdims=["pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude"]))
pn.panel(plot).servable()   # run with: panel serve notebook.ipynb
  • No changes to the visualization code — Panel wraps it as a web app
  • Deploy on EC2 or any server; users interact via browser
  • Useful when stakeholders need to explore large datasets without running Python

Datashader with Polars (Large Local Data)

import polars as pl
import datashader as ds, colorcet as cc

# scan_parquet is lazy — only reads columns and rows actually needed
df = pl.scan_parquet("s3://nyc-tlc/trip data/*.parquet").collect()

canvas = ds.Canvas(plot_width=800, plot_height=600)
agg    = canvas.points(df, "dropoff_x", "dropoff_y")
ds.tf.shade(agg, how="eq_hist", cmap=cc.fire)
  • Polars passes data to Datashader via Apache Arrow — no copy overhead
  • scan_parquet reads only the requested columns, reducing memory use
  • Faster than pandas for large Parquet reads on a single machine

Warning

Polars is single-machine. For datasets that exceed local RAM, Dask distributed across a cluster remains the right tool.

Rasterization vs. Sampling vs. Binning

Approach Scales to Preserves density Interactive zoom
Random sample + scatter ~100K No Re-sample needed
2D histogram (plt.hexbin) ~1M Yes Fixed bins
Datashader rasterize 1B+ Yes Auto re-agg
GPU (cuDF + Datashader) 10B+* Yes Yes

Sampling discards information. Rasterization summarizes all of it.

*GPU scale depends on available VRAM; numbers are from Datashader benchmarks on A100-class hardware.

Practical Considerations

Tip

Start with how="eq_hist" and a perceptually uniform colormap (viridis, fire, inferno). These two choices alone prevent most misleading density plots.

  • Projection: use projected coordinates (meters, not degrees) for geographic data — equal-area grids make pixel density meaningful
  • Canvas resolution: match plot_width / plot_height to your display resolution; a canvas that is too small hides fine structure
  • Performance: for repeated interactive use, pre-aggregate to a coarser Parquet grid and rasterize from that — avoids re-scanning raw data on every zoom

Datashader in a Spark Workflow

The Gap: Spark Produces Data, Not Pictures

  • Spark is a computation engine — it transforms, aggregates, and models data
  • Its output is a DataFrame or Parquet files on S3
  • Visualization happens downstream, after Spark finishes
  • The challenge: Spark output can still be millions of rows — too large for matplotlib
Raw S3 data
  → Spark (ETL / aggregation / MLlib)
    → Output dataset (Parquet on S3)
      → ??? → Chart

Note

Datashader does not run inside Spark. It reads Spark’s output via pandas, Polars, or Dask.

Two Bridges: Choosing the Right Path

Path 1 — Spark → Pandas

Use when Spark output fits in the driver’s memory (< ~5M rows).

Spark DataFrame
  → .toPandas()
    → Datashader
  • Fast for exploratory work
  • Single machine; RAM limit applies
  • Good for summarized / aggregated output

Path 2 — Spark → Parquet → Polars

Use when Spark output is large (> 5M rows) or will be reused.

Spark DataFrame
  → .write.parquet("s3://…")
    → pl.scan_parquet()
      → Datashader
  • Polars reads only the columns needed — fast and memory-efficient
  • Parquet files remain available for later runs
  • Single-machine; switch to Dask for distributed TB-scale data

Path 1: Spark → Pandas → Datashader

Scenario: a Spark job aggregates NYC Taxi trips by pickup location. The output is ~2M rows — small enough to collect to the driver.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
import datashader as ds, datashader.transfer_functions as tf

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

df_spark = (spark.read.parquet("s3://nyc-tlc/trip data/")
              .select("pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude", "total_amount")
              .filter("pickup_longitude != 0 AND pickup_latitude != 0"))

# Collect to driver — only safe when output is small
df = df_spark.toPandas()

canvas = ds.Canvas(plot_width=800, plot_height=600)
agg    = canvas.points(df, "pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude")
tf.shade(agg, how="eq_hist", cmap="fire")

Path 2: Spark → Parquet → Polars → Datashader

Scenario: a Spark job produces 200M enriched trip records. Too large for .toPandas() — write to S3 and read back with Polars.

# --- Spark job (runs on cluster) ---
from pyspark.sql.functions import hour
df_spark = (spark.read.parquet("s3://nyc-tlc/trip data/")
              .withColumn("hour", hour("tpep_pickup_datetime"))
              .filter("pickup_longitude != 0"))

df_spark.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("s3://my-bucket/taxi-enriched/")

# --- Visualization (runs on driver or notebook server) ---
import polars as pl
import datashader as ds, colorcet as cc

df = (pl.scan_parquet("s3://my-bucket/taxi-enriched/*.parquet",
                      storage_options={"anon": False})
        .select(["pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude", "hour"])
        .collect())

canvas = ds.Canvas(plot_width=800, plot_height=600)
agg    = canvas.points(df, "pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude")
ds.tf.shade(agg, how="eq_hist", cmap=cc.fire)

Visualizing Spark MLlib Results

Scenario: KMeans clustering on pickup coordinates. Visualize the cluster assignments to validate spatial coherence.

from pyspark.ml.clustering import KMeans
from pyspark.ml.feature import VectorAssembler

assembler = VectorAssembler(
    inputCols=["pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude"], outputCol="features")

df_feat = assembler.transform(
    df_spark.filter("pickup_longitude != 0"))

model  = KMeans(k=8, seed=42).fit(df_feat)
result = model.transform(df_feat)

# Collect predictions — one integer (cluster id) per row, lightweight
pdf = result.select("pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude", "prediction").toPandas()
pdf["prediction"] = pdf["prediction"].astype("category")

Visualizing MLlib Results — Part 2

# Color each cluster with a distinct hue
from datashader.colors import Sets1to3

canvas = ds.Canvas(plot_width=800, plot_height=600)
agg    = canvas.points(pdf, "pickup_longitude", "pickup_latitude",
                       ds.count_cat("prediction"))
img    = tf.shade(agg, color_key=Sets1to3)
tf.spread(img, px=1)
  • Each of the 8 clusters renders in a distinct color
  • Dense overlap regions alpha-blend — spatial boundaries emerge naturally
  • Validates that KMeans found geographically coherent clusters, not random splits

Tip

If cluster boundaries look jagged or arbitrary, try increasing k or re-examine the feature scaling step before the VectorAssembler.

Visualizing Big Datasets Wrap

Key Takeaways

  • The rasterization pipeline decouples data size from render cost — bottleneck is W×H, not N
  • Datashader reduces this to one call: tf.shade(canvas.points(df, x, y))
  • Integrates with Polars for fast single-machine reads, Dask for distributed TB-scale data, HoloViews/Panel for interactive dashboards
  • Mental model: you are plotting statistics of pixels, not the data itself
